name: Wendy Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Brightway, the biscuit factory by the canal. I'm on line four, which is the chocolate digestives, and my main machine is the flow-wrapper, the one that seals the biscuits into packets at about a hundred and twenty a minute. Most of the day is feeding film reels, clearing jams, checking seals and weights, and filling in the hourly sheet. When it runs well it's almost calm, like a rhythm. When the film tears you've got biscuits piling up on the belt and everyone shouting.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: There's Jen on the oven end and Kwame on the case packer, and we eat our lunch on the loading bay steps when it's not raining. I've been there six years, I'm good, not the best. Sam, my partner, drives the number nine bus, so we pass each other at the door on early shifts. Money's tight, we've got maybe two weeks' worth saved if the boiler goes again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, that's that then, back to normal. At work we'd probably laugh about the camera system they put in last year that was meant to spot broken biscuits and kept flagging shadows. Online I wouldn't bother saying much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means nothing for me changes, good or bad. I'd still be on line four, still earning less than I should, still hoping the union gets us a decent rise. I use the chatbot sometimes for letters, and that'd stay about as useful as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going. I'd carry on with the union, I'm a member but not on the committee, and I'd keep putting a bit aside when I can. Maybe I'd finally do the food safety level three course, because that gets you a bit more pay, but that's got nothing to do with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Slightly bored by the idea, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the camera that kept flagging shadows. What did that teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the stuff they sell to management is always better in the brochure. Kwame had to stand next to it for three weeks pressing 'ignore'. It works now, sort of. So I believe in it when I see it working, not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If things stayed as they are, what would you want to change about your work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Proper breaks on nights and a pay scale that actually goes up with years. I've trained four new starters and get the same rate as someone in their first month. That's the bit that annoys me, not robots.

S0.say: She'd say things are back to normal and joke at work about the camera system that kept flagging shadows as broken biscuits. She wouldn't say much online.
S0.think: She thinks nothing changes for her, good or bad: same line, same low pay, same hope for a union rise. The chatbot she uses for letters stays about as useful as it is now.
S0.do: Keeps going on line four and stays active in the union as an ordinary member. Plans to take a food safety level three course for a small pay bump, unrelated to AI.
S0.feel: Calm, and a little bored by the idea.
S0.quote: Kwame had to stand next to it for three weeks pressing 'ignore'. It works now, sort of. So I believe in it when I see it working, not before.
S0.fieldNote: Wendy's view of technology is shaped by one failed camera on her own line, which made her a 'show me first' person. Her real grievances are about pay scales and breaks. She mentioned training four new starters with no extra pay, which clearly rankles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the union needs to get ahead of this, we need training paid for and nobody pushed out without an offer. Online I might share stuff from the union page. I wouldn't be ranting, though, that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the wrapper would get smarter and they'd need fewer of us per line. Maybe one person watching two lines instead of one each. I could see myself being that person if I'm willing to learn, but I could also see them picking somebody younger and cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a few months to see what Brightway actually brings in, then I'd put my hand up for whatever training's going. If Jen or Kwame tried it first and it was alright, I'd follow. And Sam and I would stop the weekend trips to his sister's for a while and try to get the savings up to a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit nervous, but not scared. More like before an appraisal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you wait a few months rather than go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the first lot always get the broken version. With the camera, the first trainees spent weeks being blamed for its mistakes. I'd rather be second in line and learn from their swearing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sam that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably 'don't panic, it's not tomorrow.' He worries more than me. Then I'd go online and look up what the union in the other biscuit plant got, because they always get things before us.

S1.say: She'd say the union must get ahead of the change, securing paid training and making sure nobody is pushed out without an offer. She'd share union posts online but wouldn't rant.
S1.think: She expects smarter wrappers and fewer operators, perhaps one person per two lines. She could be that person if she learns, but fears the company might pick someone younger and cheaper.
S1.do: Waits a few months to see what Brightway installs, then volunteers for training once colleagues have tried it. Cuts weekend trips with Sam to build savings up to a month.
S1.feel: Nervous but not scared, like before an appraisal.
S1.quote: I'd rather be second in line and learn from their swearing.
S1.fieldNote: Wendy's 'second in line' approach is very deliberate and rooted in experience. She leans on the union as her main safety net but also plans her own training. She described herself as the calmer one at home, steadying Sam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not fair to drop this on people with two years' notice, and the government needs to guarantee incomes now. I'd be at the union meetings and I'd probably go on a march for once. I'd share a lot more online than I normally do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think the whole of line four goes. Not just me, Jen and Kwame too, the lot. If robots can do hands-on work, a biscuit line is easy. And two weeks of savings is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the food safety course and anything else quick, because some jobs might hang on a bit longer, like checking or signing things off. Sam and I would cut everything, no car, I'd sell my bike, and we'd look at moving in with my parents to save the rent. I'd sign whatever union petition and vote for whoever offers a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Proper scared, like lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd normally wait and see. Would you still?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, there's no time to be second in line. That's what's scary about this one. The way I deal with new things is to watch others first, and here there'd be nobody to watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What bill goes unpaid first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the phone contract. I'd go pay-as-you-go. Then I'd stop paying into the little pension thing work set up, which feels mad at twenty-seven, but you can't eat a pension.

S2.say: She'd say two years' notice isn't fair and that government must guarantee incomes right away. She'd attend union meetings, probably join a march and post far more than usual.
S2.think: She believes the whole of line four would go, colleagues included, since a biscuit line is easy for robots. With two weeks of savings, she sees almost no buffer.
S2.do: Takes quick courses such as food safety in case checking roles last longer. Cuts all spending, sells her bike, plans to move in with her parents, joins union campaigns and votes for a basic income.
S2.feel: Properly scared, lying awake doing sums.
S2.quote: The way I deal with new things is to watch others first, and here there'd be nobody to watch.
S2.fieldNote: The fast scenario breaks Wendy's usual method of following others, and she saw that herself. She went straight to concrete cuts, even stopping pension payments. Her politics got louder but stayed within the union and the ballot box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them properly. The union should be pushing for retraining money and a fund for people on the lines, starting now. I'd say that at meetings and to anyone at the bus stop who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'd see others try things first, which suits me. I'd still end up out of a factory job by thirty-two, I think. But I'd have time to find out what people actually need humans for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd watch closely and ask around, then by year two I'd pick a course. Maybe care work or something with people, since I'm good with new starters. I'd get the savings to two months, even if it means no holiday for a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I feel like I've got some say in it. That helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes you think care work would last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know that it would, honestly. Sam's mum is in a home and the staff there are run off their feet. I just think people would want a person holding their hand longer than they'd want a person wrapping biscuits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you watch first, to see what works?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Lena, she works in a warehouse that's already half robots. Whatever she does, I'll know if it worked by Christmas dinner. She's my early warning.

S3.say: She'd say five years should be used properly, with the union pushing now for retraining money and a fund for line workers. She'd raise it at meetings and with anyone at the bus stop.
S3.think: She likes that five years lets others go first, which suits her style. She still expects to be out of factory work by thirty-two but hopes to learn what jobs still need people.
S3.do: Watches and asks around in the first year, then chooses a course by year two, possibly in care work. Builds savings to two months by skipping holidays.
S3.feel: Worried, but helped by feeling she has some say.
S3.quote: I just think people would want a person holding their hand longer than they'd want a person wrapping biscuits.
S3.fieldNote: With some lead time, Wendy's 'watch first' habit becomes a strength, and she even named her cousin as her early warning. She was honest that she doesn't know whether care work would last. Her mood lifted noticeably once she felt she had some control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this right, so no excuses for anyone. Paid retraining, shorter weeks, and the profits from the robots shared out somehow. I'd say that at the union and I'd vote that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a decade's a long time for someone like me. I'd have time to see what works for others and then do it properly. But the end point's the same, so I'd still worry about what happens when even care homes have robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I said with the five-year one, I'd watch and then move, but slower and more carefully. I'd do the food safety course, then maybe a care qualification in the evenings around year three or four. Sam and I would try to clear his credit card and build a proper cushion, three months at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. Like I've got a map, even if I can't see the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years is long, but also that the end point is the same. How do those fit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I suppose the time helps me, and the end still frightens me. I can plan the next ten years. I can't plan what comes after, and nobody can tell me that, can they.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Sam change any big plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We talked about getting married next year, just a small thing at the registry office. I'd still do that. Kids I'd want to wait on until we know whether either of us has a job that lasts.

S4.say: She'd say ten years leaves no excuses: paid retraining, shorter weeks and robot profits shared out. She'd say it at the union and vote accordingly.
S4.think: She thinks a decade suits her, giving time to watch and then act properly. But the end point still worries her, especially if robots reach care homes too.
S4.do: Completes the food safety course, then studies for a care qualification in the evenings around year three or four. Pays off Sam's credit card and builds at least three months of savings.
S4.feel: Uneasy but steady, like having a map without seeing its end.
S4.quote: I can plan the next ten years. I can't plan what comes after, and nobody can tell me that, can they.
S4.fieldNote: Wendy separated the years before AGI, which she feels she can plan, from what comes after, which she can't. She would still marry next year but would delay children. Her answers were steady and practical, with no panic.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my whole way of coping is to watch others and learn, and there'd be no time for that. What would help is a guaranteed income while people retrain, and the training actually paid, not just a website. And honestly, a union that's at the table when the robots get bought, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people who train the new starters. That's the part of my job I'm proud of. If there are robots, someone still has to show the humans around them, and I'd like that to count for something.

headlineQuote: If there are robots, someone still has to show the humans around them, and I'd like that to count for something.
portrait: Wendy is a 27-year-old flow-wrapper operator on the chocolate digestive line at a canal-side biscuit factory, living with her partner Sam, a bus driver, on about two weeks of savings. One failed camera system on her line made her a 'show me first' person who prefers to be second in line. She leans on the union and votes for shared gains, but she also makes her own plans, from a food safety course to possible care work. The two-year scenario frightens her most because it removes the time she needs to watch others, while ten years feels like a map, even if she can't see where it ends.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because her way of coping is to watch others first and learn, and there would be no time for that.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed income during retraining, training that is actually paid for, and a union at the table when the robots are bought.
